name: image
description: Image as the slide's anchor, with optional text alongside — composition adapts to the asset and the deck.
purpose: Use when a visual carries meaning on its own. You hand it any rectangle; the layout reads the asset's aspect at build time and, with the deck orientation, RESOLVES the composition for you — no modifier needed. The default is `clean` (a floated card shaped to the photo, ≈ zero crop); extreme aspects auto-pick `split` (shown whole) or `spotlight` (full-bleed cover). Name a composition to override: `clean` · `split` · `spotlight` · `gallery` (contain-on-matte, for diagrams) · `statement` (full-bleed + scrim + title). `mirror` flips the image side. On `spotlight` and `statement`, the text card takes its own `image-card-*` classes: placement (`image-card-top-right` and six more), backing (`image-card-solid`/`soft`/`sheer`/`clear`, or any 5% step such as `image-card-65`), ink (`image-card-light`/`dark`), size (`image-card-sm`/`md`/`lg`), density (`image-card-compact`) and shape (`image-card-band` stretches the card across the top or bottom edge); the deck front-matter `image-card:` sets them for every image slide in one line. Legacy `full`/`contain`/`museum` still work (→ spotlight/gallery/gallery).

image.description: The photo, as Markdown's picture alone on its line: `![A name](path "A longer description")`. The slide places it on its photo panel (`mirror` moves the panel to the left). To try a composition before you have the photo, use a sample: `![A lake at dusk](sample:photo-wide.svg)`, or `photo-tall`, `photo-pano` and `photo-square` (the full set is in `lib/samples/README.md`). The `@image{…}` record places the same way and takes a frame, a finish and a tone.

heading.description: Optional heading in the text slot.

skeleton:
<!-- @meta{layout=image} -->

## Text leads; the image earns its place.

Swap the picture below for your own photo, and name it — any aspect. The layout reads its shape and resolves the composition for you (a floated card, a full-height column, a full-bleed cover). Name a composition (`image spotlight`, `image gallery`, …) only to override.

![A figure by a lake under a low sun](sample:photo-wide.svg)

<!-- @meta{layout=image} -->

## The image layout reads the asset’s shape.

Two-thirds of trials that reach the first generated report convert to paid; the ones that stall at workspace setup almost never do. Hand the layout any photo — it resolves the composition from the asset's shape.

![A figure by a lake under a low sun](sample:photo-wide.svg)

whenToUse.title: The visual carries meaning
whenToUse.body: Product screenshots, architectural photographs, plots, satellite imagery — anywhere the image makes the argument and the prose is annotation. If the visual is decorative, drop it and use `content` instead.

whenToUse.title: Let the layout resolve it — override only with intent
whenToUse.body: Drop in any aspect and the layout reads it: a moderate photo gets the `clean` floated card, a tall/wide one gets `split` (shown whole), a canvas-matching one gets `spotlight` (full-bleed). Override only when you mean it: `image gallery` to contain a diagram zero-crop, `image statement` for a scrim-and-title hero, `image spotlight` to force a full-bleed cover (accepting the crop).

whenToUse.title: Caption earns its line
whenToUse.body: If the prose alongside the image just describes what the image shows, drop it — the audience can see the picture. The text slot is for the so-what: what the audience should take away from the visual.

antiPatterns.title: Decorative stock photo
antiPatterns.body: A generic photograph of 'people in a meeting' next to a content slide is filler. Use `content` and trust the prose; reserve image for visuals that argue for themselves.

antiPatterns.title: Image too small to read
antiPatterns.body: A diagram or screenshot small enough to fit inside a half-canvas text slot is unreadable from the back of the room. Reach for `image gallery` (contains it whole) or `image spotlight`, or move the diagram to its own `diagram` slide.

antiPatterns.title: Image with five paragraphs of caption
antiPatterns.body: If the prose dominates and the image is a sidebar, you have a `content` slide that happens to have a photo. Either trust the image (drop the prose) or trust the prose (drop the image).

related.name: diagram
related.when: the visual is a Mermaid graph, not a photo or screenshot

related.name: content
related.when: the slide is mostly prose with one inline visual

related.name: title
related.when: the image is a bookend hero, not the body of a slide

related.name: quote
related.when: the slide is a quotation, not an image

commonMistakes.mistake: Giving the photo a second lone picture, or putting Marp's side keywords in its alt (`![bg left](path)`).
commonMistakes.fix: The photo is the slide's ONE lone picture: `![A name](path "A longer description")` alone on its line, or `@image{path, title="…"}`. The slide places it on its panel, and `mirror` moves it to the left. A second lone picture, or a `![bg]` or record already on the slide, keeps the other picture in the text, and an `http:` address is not placed (use `https:`). `lint:deck --fix` rewrites an old `![bg …]` line into the picture and the slide's class.

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming a composition class (`image spotlight`, `image gallery`, …) reflexively instead of leaving it unset.
commonMistakes.fix: The composition RESOLVES from the photo's own aspect ratio plus the deck orientation — an explicit class always wins over the resolver, so naming one out of habit can force a crop (e.g. `spotlight`'s full-bleed cover) that the auto-picked `clean`/`split` composition would have avoided.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding a card control (`image-card-*`) to a `clean`, `split` or `gallery` slide.
commonMistakes.fix: Those compositions set the text beside the photo, not over it, so there is no card to move. The card controls act only on `spotlight` and `statement` — name one of those first: `image spotlight image-card-top-right image-card-sm`.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: The photo has a moderate, unremarkable aspect — the safe default; leave the class off and let the resolver land here for near-zero crop.
The photo has an extreme aspect — a tall portrait or a full panorama — and must be shown whole, uncropped, in its own column or band.
The photo already matches the canvas's own aspect and can carry the whole slide full-bleed, with a solid text card guaranteeing legibility over it.
The asset is a diagram or screenshot where whitespace and containment are the point — mats it whole on a matte with a placard, zero crop.
You want an editorial scrim-and-title hero treatment — a deliberate full-bleed gamble rather than the safe legible default.
The composition is right but the deck's rhythm wants the image on the left instead of the right — flips the side without changing the composition.

On `spotlight` or `statement`, the photo's subject sits where the card would land — move the card to the quiet part of the frame with one of `image-card-top-left` · `image-card-top` · `image-card-top-right` · `image-card-center` · `image-card-bottom-left` · `image-card-bottom` · `image-card-bottom-right`.

On `spotlight` or `statement`, the backing hides too much photo — thin it with `image-card-soft` (80%) or `image-card-sheer` (55%), set an exact level with a 5% step (`image-card-65` is 65%; the deck line writes `65%`), or drop it with `image-card-clear` when the photo is calm where the words land. A thin spotlight card (under 60%) needs a matching `image-card-light` or `image-card-dark`, or the theme's own ink is read against the photo; lint warns (`thin-card-no-ink`), and in the Studio the Card backing slider picks one from the photo for you.
On `spotlight` or `statement`, the photo is bright where the words land — `image-card-dark` sets dark words on a light backing; `image-card-light` sets white words on a dark one.

On `spotlight` or `statement`, the card competes with the photo — `image-card-sm` shrinks the card and its type so the photo carries the slide; `image-card-lg` does the opposite. Add `image-card-compact` to tighten the card's padding and pull it closer to the slide edge at any size.

On `spotlight` or `statement`, the card covers something you want to see above or below it — add `image-card-band` to `image-card-top` or `image-card-bottom` to stretch the card across the slide in one short strip (heading left, text right) and leave the middle of the photo clear, with a hairline in the gap between the two columns. On a corner or center placement `image-card-band` does nothing; `image-card-float` steps one slide out of a deck-wide band.

media.describe: The `image` slide makes its one picture the photo panel and picks the composition from the photo's shape (`mirror` puts it on the left). A finish, a tone and `focus=` apply to the panel; it has no frame and no size of its own, because the panel runs to the composition's edges.
